extra_misconceptions.fact: Dry reed cracks into razor-sharp splinters when bent; warm water soaking softens the fibers so they flex safely without snapping.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Weaving with dry, unsoaked flat reed prevents mold growth and reduces the chance of sharp edge splinters on your fingers.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Drawing long reed strands toward your face risks serious eye scratches; always pull weavers away from your body and fellow Scouts.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pulling a long weaver strand directly toward your face lets you apply tighter, more accurate tension on the basket rim.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Hydrogen peroxide damages healthy healing tissue; flush minor cuts with clean running water, wash with soap, and apply a bandage.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pouring hydrogen peroxide into a fresh reed cut sterilizes the wound faster than washing with mild soap and clean water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Over-soaking reed turns the fibers mushy, causes gray mildew stains, and weakens the strands so they snap unpredictably under load.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Leaving soaked reed bundles submerged in water overnight makes them extra pliable and safer to weave the next morning.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to brittle reed fibers if you cut or bend them before soaking them in warm water for the required time?
Which physical indicator distinguishes a deep reed-splinter puncture requiring sterile tweezers from a surface scratch?
What measurement confirms that your workbench spacing gives each weaver a safe blood circle when swinging long spokes?
Why is it dangerous to trim protruding basket spokes with a dull pocketknife instead of sharp diagonal reed cutters?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Coiled basketry is a sewing technique where a flexible needle strand wraps and stitches a continuous spiral core bundle together.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Coiled baskets are woven by interlacing stiff vertical spokes with horizontal reed weavers in an alternating pattern.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Continuous over-under weaving with one strand requires an odd number of stakes so each new circuit alternates over and under.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Single-weaver randing around a round basket works identically whether the base has an even or an odd number of stakes.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Plaited baskets interlace flat, uniform strips of equal width at right angles or diagonals, serving as both base and sidewalls.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Plaited baskets require rigid round reed spokes because flat strips cannot support the weight of the basket sidewalls.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Twining uses two or more flexible weavers that twist a half-turn around each other between every vertical stake to lock it in place.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Twining is simply another name for weaving a single flat reed over two stakes and under one stake in a diagonal twill.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to the vertical stakes in a wicker basket when you switch from simple over-under randing to two-rod twining?
Which structural feature distinguishes a coiled basket sewn over a flexible core from a woven wicker or ribbed basket?
What stake count requirement confirms that a continuous single-weaver over-under pattern will alternate rows properly?
Where should a Scout position their non-dominant hand when pushing a sharp basketry awl through a tight coiled bundle?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Over-tightening weavers pulls the corner stakes inward into an hourglass shape; steady, gentle shaping keeps the sidewalls vertical.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pulling every horizontal weaver as tightly as possible gives a square basket straighter corners and vertical sidewalls.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Reed shrinks as it dries, so wrapping wet campstool strands too tightly can bow or crack the wooden frame dowels as they dry.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Wrapping the warp strands of a campstool seat with maximum tension while wet prevents the seat from sagging later.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Spoke ends must extend past at least two or three horizontal rows on the inside wall so friction locks the rim securely in place.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tucking trimmed spoke ends only one row deep into the rim is sufficient to hold a round basket border under heavy loads.

extra_misconceptions.fact: All splices, knots, and overlapping reed ends on a campstool seat belong on the underside so the sitting surface stays smooth.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Starting the second layer of a campstool seat requires splicing new strands directly onto the top surface of the rails.

extra_socratic_questions: Under what condition does crimping flat reed stakes at a ninety-degree angle allow a square basket base to stand upright?
Which structural difference explains why a campstool seat wraps warp strands around wooden rails instead of slotted bases?
What measurement confirms that your square basket base is truly square before you crimp and bend up the side stakes?
Why is it dangerous to sit on a newly woven campstool before the wet reed fibers have completely dried and shrunk tight?
